title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 107
paragraphs: Meanwhile, those barbarians who had escaped and been driven to the heights of Mycale — being not many in number — were making their way to Sardis. As they went, Masistes son of Darius, who had been present at the disaster that befell them, was saying many harsh things of the commander Artaÿntes — among others, that he had shown himself worse than a woman in his generalship, and deserved every kind of evil for having brought evil on the king's house. Now for Persians, to be called worse than a woman is the greatest possible reproach. So Artaÿntes, after much reviling, at length grew angry and drew his sword on Masistes, meaning to kill him. As he was running at him, Xeinagoras son of Prexilaos, a man of Halicarnassus, who was standing just behind Artaÿntes, perceived it; he seized him round the waist and, lifting him up, dashed him to the ground, and meanwhile Masistes's spearmen came in front to protect him. Thus did Xeinagoras, and thus he laid up thanks for himself both with Masistes and with Xerxes for saving the life of his brother; for this deed Xeinagoras became ruler of all Cilicia by the king's gift. Nothing further happened on the way, and they reached Sardis.
Now at Sardis, as it happened, King Xerxes had been staying ever since the time he came there in flight from Athens, after his defeat in the sea-fight.
